definitions.text: Never mounted by a rider; unbroken. "Unbacked colts." Shak.
Not supported or encouraged; not countenanced; unaided. Daniel.
To pour, or take, or let go, out of a bag or bags.
Not balanced; not in equipoise; having no counterpoise, or having insufficient counterpoise. Let Earth unbalanced from her orbit fly. Pope.
(Com.)
Not adjusted; not settled; not brought to an equality of debt and credit; as, an unbalanced account; unbalanced books.
Being, or being thrown, out of equilibrium; hence, disordered or deranged in sense; unsteady; unsound; as, an unbalanced mind. Pope.
To free from ballast; to discharge ballast from. Totten.
Not ballasted. [Obs. & R.] Addison.
Etym: [Properly p. p. unballast.]
Freed from ballast; having discharged ballast.
Etym: [Pref. un- not + ballasted.]
Not furnished with ballast; not kept steady by ballast; unsteady; as, unballasted vessels; unballasted wits. Unballasted by any sufficient weight of plan. De Quincey.
Wanting a band or string; unfastened. [Obs.] Shak.
To remove a bank from; to open by, or as if by, the removal of a bank. H. Taylor.
To remove a bar or bars from; to unbolt; to open; as, to unbar a gate. Heber.
Not shaven. [Obs.]
Destitute of bards, or of reversed points, hairs, or plumes; as, an unbarded feather.
To deprive of the bark; to decorticate; to strip; as, to unbark a tree. Bacon.
To cause to disembark; to land. [Obs.] Hakluyt.
To remove or release from a barrel or barrels.
To unbolt; to unbar; to open. You shall not unbarricade the door. J. Webster (1623).
Not obstructed by barricades; open; as, unbarricadoed streets. Burke.
Not bashful or modest; bold; impudent; shameless. Shak.
To free from the restraint of anything that surrounds or incloses; to let loose; to open. [Obs.] I ought . . . to unbay the current of my passion. Norris.
To cause not to be; to cause to be another. [Obs. & R.] How oft, with danger of the field beset, Or with home mutinies, would he unbe Himself! Old Pay.
To remove or loose the bearing rein of (a horse).
To deliver from the form or nature of a beast.
To misbecome. [Obs.] Bp. Sherlock.
Not becoming; unsuitable; unfit; indecorous; improper.
To raise or rouse from bed. Eels unbed themselves and stir at the noise of thunder. Wa
Not filled with din.
To deliver from the state of a fool; to awaken the mind of; to undeceive.
To deprive of existence. Dryden.
Not gilded; hence, not rewarded with gold.
Not begot; not yet generated; also, having never been generated; self-existent; eternal.
To set free from the influence of guile; to undeceive. "Then unbeguile thyself." Donne.
Not yet begun; also, existing without a beginning.
Not behooving or becoming; unseemly. [Obs. & R.] Gower.
Not existing. [Obs.] "Beings yet unbeing." Sir T. Browne.
Not known; unknown. [Colloq.]
The withholding of belief; doubt; incredulity; skepticism.
Disbelief; especially, disbelief of divine revelation, or in a divine providence or scheme of redemption. Blind unbelief is sure to err, And scan his work in vain. Cowper.
Not believed; disbelieved.
One who does not believe; an incredulous person; a doubter; a skeptic.
A disbeliever; especially, one who does not believe that the Bible is a divine revelation, and holds that Christ was neither a divine nor a supernatural person; an infidel; a freethinker.
Not believing; incredulous; doubting; distrusting; skeptical.
Believing the thing alleged no to be true; disbelieving; especially, believing that Bible is not a divine revelation, or that Christ was not a divine or a supernatural person. "Unbelieving Jews."
To remove or loose the belt of; to ungird.
To free from flexure; to make, or allow to become, straight; to loosen; as, to unbend a bow.
A remit from a strain or from exertion; to set at ease for a time; to relax; as, to unbend the mind from study or care. You do unbend your noble strength. Shak.
(Naut.) (a) To unfasten, as sails, from the spars or stays to which they are attached for use. (b) To cast loose or untie, as a rope.
To cease to be bent; to become straight or relaxed.
To relax in exertion, attention, severity, or the like; hence, to indulge in mirth or amusement.
Not bending; not suffering flexure; not yielding to pressure; stiff; -- applied to material things. Flies o'er unbending corn, and skims along the main. Pope.
Unyielding in will; not subject to persuasion or influence; inflexible; resolute; -- applied to persons.
Unyielding in nature; unchangeable; fixed; -- applied to abstract ideas; as, unbending truths.
Devoted to relaxation or amusement. [R.]
Absence or want of benevolence; ill will.
Not benign; malignant.
To relieve of numbness; to restore sensation to.
Unbereft. [R.]
Not bereft; not taken away.
To be unbecoming or unsuitable to; to misbecome.
To unsay; hence, to annul or cancel. [Obs.] Pepys.
To change the mind of (one's self). [Obs.]
Unawares. [Obs.] Bale.
To free from a spell; to disenchant. [R.] South.
To free from bias or prejudice. Swift.
Not bidden; not commanded. Thorns also and thistles it shall bring thee forth Unbid; and thou shalt eat the herb of the field. Milton.
Uninvited; as, unbidden guests. Shak.
Being without a prayer. [Obs.] Spenser.
To remove a band from; to set free from shackles or fastenings; to unite; to unfasten; to loose; as, unbind your fillets; to unbind a prisoner's arms; to unbind a load.
To deprive, as a city, of a bishop; to deprive, as a clergyman, of episcopal dignity or rights. [R.] "Then he unbishops himself." Milton.
To remove the turns of (a rope or cable) from the bits; as, to unbit a cable. Totten.
Not blemished; pure; spotless; as, an unblemished reputation or life. Addison.
To deprive of blessings; to make wretched. [Obs.] Shak.
Not blest; excluded from benediction; hence, accursed; wretched. "Unblessed enchanter." Milton.
Unblessed. [R.] Sylvester.
To free from blindness; to give or restore sight to; to open the eyes of. [R.] J. Webster (1607).
To free from that which blindfolds. Spenser.
Not bloody. Dryden. Unbloody sacrifice. (a) A sacrifice in which no victim is slain. (b) (R. C. Ch.) The Mass.
To free from the body; to disembody. Her soul unbodied of the burdenous corse. Spenser.
To leave the body; to be disembodied; -- said of the soul or spirit. [R.] Chaucer.
To remove a bolt from; to unfasten; to unbar; to open. "He shall unbolt the gates." Shak.
To explain or unfold a matter; to make a revelation. [Obs.] "I will unbolt to you." Shak.
To deprive of bones, as meat; to bone.
To twist about, as if boneless. [R.] Milton.
To take a bonnet from; to take off one's bonnet; to uncover; as, to unbonnet one's head. Sir W. Scott.
Not written in a book; unrecorded. "UnbookedEnglish life." Masson.
To take off the boots from.
Not born; no yet brought into life; being still to appear; future. Some unborn sorrow, ripe in fortune's womb. Shak. See future sons, and daughters yet unborn. Pope.
Not borrowed; being one's own; native; original.
To disclose freely; to reveal in confidence, as secrets; to confess; -- often used reflexively; as, to unbosom one's self. Milton.
One who unbosoms, or discloses. [R.] "An unbosomer of secrets." Thackeray.
Etym: [1st pref. un- + bottom + -ed.]
Deprived of a bottom.
Etym: [Pref. un- not + bottomed.]
Having no bottom; bottomless. Milton.
imp. & p. p. of Unbind.
Infinitely. [Obs.] I am . . . unboundably beholding to you. J. Webster (1607).
Having no bound or limit; as, unbounded space; an, unbounded
To unbend. [R.] Fuller.
Not bent or arched; not bowed down. Byron.
To deprive of the entrails; to disembowel. Dr. H. More.
To remove from a box or boxes.
To divest of the traits of a boy. [R.] Clarendon.
To free from tension; to relax; to loose; as, to unbrace a drum; to unbrace the nerves. Spenser.
To separate the strands of; to undo, as a braid; to unravel; to disentangle.
To disclose, or lay open; to unbosom. [Obs.] P. Fletcher,
Not breathed.
Not exercised; unpracticed. [Obs.] "Their unbreathed memories." Shak.
Not begotten; unborn. [Obs.] "Thou age unbred." Shak.
Not taught or trained; -- with to. Dryden.
Not well-bred; ill-bred. [Obs.] Locke.
To remove the breeches of; to divest or strip of breeches. Shak.
(Gun.)
To free the breech of, as a cannon, from its fastenings or coverings. Pennant.
Not made by brewing; unmixed; pure; genuine. [R.] Young.
To free from the bridle; to set loose.
Loosed from the bridle, or as from the bridle; hence, unrestrained; licentious; violent; as, unbridled passions. "Unbridled boldness." B. Jonson.
Not broken; continuous; unsubdued; as, an unbroken colt.
To loose the buckles of; to unfasten; as, to unbuckle a shoe. "Unbuckle anon thy purse." Chaucer.
To demolish; to raze. "To unbuild the city." Shak.
To release, as from a bundle; to disclose.
To remove the bung from; as, to unbung a cask.
To relieve from a burden.
To throw off, as a burden; to unload.
Not ready or not proper to be buried. Tennyson.
To force from a burrow; to unearth.
To unburden; to unload.
To disinter; to exhume; fig., to disclose.
Not required to work; unemployed; not busy. [R.] These unbusied persons can continue in this playing idleness till it become a toil. Bp. Rainbow
To loose the buttons of; to unfasten.
Disobedient. [Obs.] Piers Plowman.
